blocks.text: A milk jug made of high-density polyethylene bends easily in the hand and softens in boiling water, while a PEEK bearing cage in a jet engine accessory gearbox runs at 200 C for thousands of hours. Both are 'plastics' built from long carbon-chain molecules; the difference lies in how long the chains are, how neatly they pack and how strongly they are linked.

blocks.markdown: A polymer is a collection of long chain molecules built by repeating a small unit (the mer). Unlike a metal or a pure compound, a polymer sample contains chains of many different lengths, so a single molecular weight is meaningless; we describe the distribution by averages. The properties of a thermoplastic are then controlled by three structural features: molecular weight, degree of crystallinity and crosslinking.

blocks.title: Number- and weight-average molecular weight
blocks.text: The **number-average** molecular weight $\overline{M}_n$ is the total mass of polymer divided by the number of chains, weighting each chain equally. The **weight-average** molecular weight $\overline{M}_w$ weights each chain by its mass, so long chains count more. The ratio $\overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n\ge1$ is the **polydispersity index** (PDI); a value of 1 means all chains have identical length.

blocks.caption: x_i is the number fraction and w_i the weight (mass) fraction of chains in size range i with mean molecular weight M_i (g per mol). The degree of polymerisation is DP = Mn / m, with m the mer molecular weight.

blocks.title: Averages from a number-fraction distribution
blocks.prompt: A polymer has the following distribution of number fractions $x_i$ at mean molecular weights $M_i$: 0.10 at 10 000, 0.30 at 20 000, 0.40 at 30 000 and 0.20 at 50 000 g mol$^{-1}$. Calculate $\overline{M}_n$, $\overline{M}_w$ and the PDI.

steps.text: For the weight average with number fractions use $\sum x_iM_i^{2}/\sum x_iM_i$, so first sum $x_iM_i^{2}$.

blocks.answer: Mn = 29 000 g/mol, Mw about 34 100 g/mol, PDI about 1.18 (Mw is always larger than Mn when chains differ in length).

blocks.markdown: **Molecular weight and properties.** Longer chains entangle more, so strength, toughness and melt viscosity rise with molecular weight, though the gain levels off at a high value. Polyethylene of $\overline{M}_n\approx30\,000$ is a typical moulding grade and ultra-high-molecular-weight grades reach millions, giving exceptional wear resistance but poor melt flow.

**Crystallinity.** In a semi-crystalline thermoplastic, regions of regularly folded chains (crystallites) are embedded in disordered amorphous material. Higher crystallinity gives higher density, stiffness, strength, hardness and chemical resistance, a higher melting temperature, and lower transparency and ductility. Crystallinity is favoured by regular, unbranched chains (high-density polyethylene is more crystalline than branched low-density polyethylene), by strong secondary bonding and by slow cooling. A fully amorphous polymer such as polystyrene has only a glass transition, no true melting point.

blocks.caption: rho is the measured density of the sample, rho_c the density of the fully crystalline polymer and rho_a that of the fully amorphous polymer (all in g per cm^3).

blocks.title: Crystallinity of two polyethylenes
blocks.prompt: For polyethylene take $\rho_c=1.00$ g cm$^{-3}$ and $\rho_a=0.85$ g cm$^{-3}$ (typical). Find the crystallinity of a high-density grade with $\rho=0.96$ g cm$^{-3}$ and a low-density grade with $\rho=0.92$ g cm$^{-3}$.

steps.text: Interpretation: the unbranched high-density chains pack more regularly, so the high-density grade is more crystalline, stiffer and has a higher melting point (about 130 C against about 110 C, typical).

blocks.answer: About 76 % crystalline for the high-density grade and about 51 % for the low-density grade.

blocks.markdown: **Crosslinking.** A crosslink is a covalent bond between chains. A low density of crosslinks (vulcanised rubber) stops chains slipping past each other, gives elastic recovery and raises the stiffness a little; a high density (epoxy, phenolic) produces a rigid network that cannot melt or flow, so it decomposes on heating instead. Crosslinking raises the stiffness and the glass transition temperature and reduces the extensibility, and it prevents melting: a crosslinked polymer (thermoset) is not remoulded by reheating.

rows: Little change; strength and toughness increase
Tm roughly constant; melt viscosity rises strongly
blocks.caption: Trends only; the size of each effect depends on the polymer.

blocks.markdown: **Engineering thermoplastics.** Polyethylene is cheap, tough, chemically resistant and slippery but soft and limited to low temperatures. Nylon 6,6 is stronger and stiffer because the amide groups form hydrogen bonds between chains, raising the melting point, but it absorbs water, which plasticises it and lowers its stiffness. PEEK has stiff aromatic rings and ether and ketone links in its backbone, giving high strength, a glass transition near 143 C and continuous use to about 250 C, with excellent chemical resistance but high cost.

rows: High temperature and chemical resistance, costly
blocks.caption: Representative values of typical grades; check a data sheet for design.

blocks.title: Link structure to property
blocks.text: For any question on a polymer, ask: (i) how long are the chains (molecular weight), (ii) how regularly do they pack (crystallinity, branching, bulky side groups), (iii) are they linked (crosslinks), and (iv) how strong are the secondary bonds (hydrogen bonding, polar groups, stiff rings)? Higher regularity, crosslinking and stronger secondary bonding give higher stiffness and higher softening temperature.

points: Molecular weight is a distribution: $\overline{M}_n=\sum x_iM_i$, $\overline{M}_w=\sum w_iM_i$ and PDI $=\overline{M}_w/\overline{M}_n\ge1$.
Higher crystallinity raises density, stiffness and melting temperature but lowers ductility and transparency; crosslinking raises stiffness and suppresses melting, giving thermosets.
HDPE is cheap and tough but soft; nylon 6,6 is stronger because of hydrogen bonds but absorbs moisture; PEEK has the highest temperature capability and chemical resistance at high cost.

questions.stem: A semi-crystalline polyethylene is processed so that its crystallinity increases from 50 % to 70 % with no other change. Which set of changes is expected?

options.text: Lower density, higher stiffness and lower ductility
Higher density, lower stiffness and a lower melting point
Higher density, stiffness and melting point, lower ductility
No change in stiffness, since only the amorphous regions carry load

questions.correctOptionText: Higher density, stiffness and melting point, lower ductility

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: crystalline regions are denser than amorphous ones, so density rises.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: increasing the crystalline fraction stiffens the polymer and does not lower the melting point.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: more tightly packed crystallites raise density, stiffness and melting point, while the reduced amorphous fraction lowers the ductility.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the crystallites are stiffer than the amorphous matrix and carry much of the load.

questions.explanation: Crystalline regions have denser, regular packing with strong secondary bonding, so their increase raises density, modulus, yield strength and melting temperature. The amorphous regions give the toughness and ductility, so a smaller amorphous fraction reduces them.

questions.stem: How does a light level of crosslinking, as in vulcanised rubber, change the behaviour of a polymer compared with the same polymer uncrosslinked?

options.text: It prevents the chains from flowing past each other, giving elastic recovery and no melting flow
It increases the crystallinity and so raises the density
It lowers the glass transition temperature by loosening the chains
It makes the polymer thermoplastic so it can be remoulded

questions.correctOptionText: It prevents the chains from flowing past each other, giving elastic recovery and no melting flow

distractorRationale.a: Correct: crosslinks tie the chains into a network, which stops viscous flow and gives elastic recovery.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: crosslinks disrupt, rather than promote, regular packing.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: crosslinks restrict chain motion and so raise the glass transition.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a crosslinked polymer cannot be melted and remoulded, which is the defining behaviour of a thermoset.

questions.explanation: Covalent bonds between chains form a network that cannot flow. With a few crosslinks the segments between them are still mobile, so the material is elastic, whereas a high crosslink density gives a stiff, brittle thermoset.

questions.stem: Nylon 6,6 melts at about 265 C whereas polyethylene melts at about 130 C, although both are linear semi-crystalline polymers. What is the main reason?

options.text: Nylon has a much shorter chain length, which raises its melting point
Nylon is crosslinked while polyethylene is not
Polyethylene contains aromatic rings that weaken the crystal
Hydrogen bonding between amide groups on neighbouring chains holds the crystal together more strongly

questions.correctOptionText: Hydrogen bonding between amide groups on neighbouring chains holds the crystal together more strongly

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: short chains would lower, not raise, the melting point.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: nylon 6,6 is a linear thermoplastic that melts, so it is not crosslinked.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: polyethylene has a simple saturated carbon backbone with no aromatic rings.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: hydrogen bonds between amide groups raise the energy needed to disrupt the crystal.

questions.explanation: Polyethylene chains are held by weak van der Waals forces, so the crystal melts at a low temperature. The amide groups in nylon form hydrogen bonds between chains, which add strong secondary bonding and raise both stiffness and melting point.

questions.stem: A polyethylene sample has measured density 0.94 g cm$^{-3}$. Take the fully crystalline density as 1.00 g cm$^{-3}$ and the fully amorphous density as 0.85 g cm$^{-3}$. Calculate its percentage crystallinity.
questions.explanation: Using $X_c=\rho_c(\rho-\rho_a)/[\rho(\rho_c-\rho_a)]$ gives $X_c=1.00\times0.09/(0.94\times0.15)=0.09/0.141=0.638$, so the crystallinity is 63.8 %. This is lower than the 76 % of the high-density grade in the lesson, as expected for a lower density.

questions.stem: A polymer sample has number fractions of 0.40 at $M=5000$, 0.40 at $M=15000$ and 0.20 at $M=25000$ g mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the weight-average molecular weight $\overline{M}_w=\sum x_iM_i^{2}/\sum x_iM_i$, in g mol$^{-1}$.

A polymer has weight fractions of 0.20 at $M=8000$, 0.50 at $M=20000$ and 0.30 at $M=40000$ g mol$^{-1}$. Calculate the number-average molecular weight, using $\overline{M}_n=1/\sum(w_i/M_i)$, in g mol$^{-1}$.
questions.explanation: The sum is $\sum w_i/M_i=0.2/8000+0.5/20000+0.3/40000=2.5\times10^{-5}+2.5\times10^{-5}+7.5\times10^{-6}=5.75\times10^{-5}$ mol g$^{-1}$. Therefore $\overline{M}_n=1/5.75\times10^{-5}=17400$ g mol$^{-1}$; the weight average of the same sample is 23 600, so the PDI is 1.36.

questions.stem: Which statement about the molecular-weight averages of a polymer sample is correct?

options.text: $\overline{M}_n\ge\overline{M}_w$ for every sample
$\overline{M}_w\ge\overline{M}_n$, with equality only if all chains have the same length
$\overline{M}_w$ and $\overline{M}_n$ are always equal for a thermoplastic
The PDI can be less than 1 for a very narrow distribution

questions.correctOptionText: $\overline{M}_w\ge\overline{M}_n$, with equality only if all chains have the same length

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the number average weights short chains as much as long ones and so is smaller or equal.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: weighting by mass gives greater importance to long chains, so the weight average is never smaller than the number average.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: they are equal only for a monodisperse sample, which a synthetic thermoplastic essentially never is.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the ratio of the two is at least 1 by definition; 1 means identical chain lengths.

questions.explanation: The weight average gives more weight to heavy chains, so $\overline{M}_w=\sum x_iM_i^{2}/\sum x_iM_i$ is at least $\overline{M}_n=\sum x_iM_i$. The ratio, the PDI, equals 1 only if every chain has the same mass.

questions.stem: A bushing must run dry against a steel shaft at 200 C continuous temperature in a chemically aggressive environment. Which of HDPE, nylon 6,6 and PEEK is the best choice, and why?

options.text: HDPE, because its low friction is the most important property
Nylon 6,6, because it has the highest melting temperature
None of them, since all thermoplastics melt below 100 C
PEEK, because its glass transition and continuous-use temperature are well above 200 C and its chemical resistance is excellent

questions.correctOptionText: PEEK, because its glass transition and continuous-use temperature are well above 200 C and its chemical resistance is excellent

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: HDPE melts at about 130 C and is far too soft at 200 C.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: nylon 6,6 melts at about 265 C but its use temperature is only about 100 to 120 C, and it absorbs moisture.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: PEEK melts at about 343 C, so thermoplastics can exceed 200 C.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: PEEK retains its strength to around 250 C and resists most chemicals.

questions.explanation: The design temperature of 200 C rules out HDPE and nylon 6,6, whose continuous-use temperatures are about 80 C and 100 to 120 C. PEEK, with a glass transition near 143 C and continuous use to about 250 C, retains useful stiffness and resists chemicals, but at a higher cost.

questions.stem: Explain how crystallinity and crosslink density affect the stiffness and the melting or softening behaviour of a polymer. Give a polymer example for each of high crystallinity, light crosslinking and heavy crosslinking.
markingGuide: Crystallinity: regular packing and secondary bonding in crystallites give higher modulus, density and melting temperature, but lower ductility and transparency
Example of high crystallinity: HDPE (about 76 % crystalline, melting near 130 C) or nylon 6,6
Crosslinking: covalent links between chains form a network that stops viscous flow
Light crosslinking (for example vulcanised rubber): elastic, with large reversible extension and no flow
Heavy crosslinking (for example epoxy or phenolic thermoset): rigid and brittle, with no melting, and it decomposes on heating
Notes that crosslinking raises the glass transition and stiffness, whereas amorphous polymers soften at Tg rather than melt sharply
questions.explanation: Both structural features restrict chain motion: crystallinity by regular packing and crosslinking by covalent bonds. The more the motion is restricted, the stiffer the polymer and the higher its softening temperature, but the lower its ductility.

questions.stem: Compare polyethylene, nylon 6,6 and PEEK for engineering use, in terms of structure, stiffness, strength and temperature capability, and suggest one application for each. In addition, a polyethylene sample has $\overline{M}_n=56\,100$ g/mol and a mer (C$_2$H$_4$) weight of 28.05 g/mol: calculate its degree of polymerisation.
markingGuide: Polyethylene: simple saturated carbon chain with weak van der Waals bonding; low modulus (about 1 GPa) and strength (25 to 30 MPa), melts near 130 C; application: pipes, films, containers

Nylon 6,6: amide groups form hydrogen bonds; higher modulus (2.5 to 3 GPa) and strength (about 70 to 80 MPa) dry, melts near 265 C, but absorbs moisture which reduces stiffness; application: gears, bearings

PEEK: stiff aromatic rings with ether and ketone links; modulus about 3.6 GPa, strength about 100 MPa, Tg about 143 C, use to about 250 C, chemical resistance, high cost; application: aerospace and high-temperature bearings
Selection logic: match temperature, load and cost
Degree of polymerisation of the polyethylene: DP = Mn / mer weight = 56 100 / 28.05 = 2000
questions.explanation: The three polymers lie on a spectrum of increasing secondary bonding and chain stiffness, which raises their strength and temperature capability and also their cost. The degree of polymerisation is the average mass of the chain divided by the mass of the repeat unit.
